studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops comparing similar themes and patterns of events across cultures within the unit “In-Depth Study: Character, Setting, Event, and Point of View.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's transfer challenge work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
I had been at the station for three weeks before anyone let me touch the board.

My job was the log. Every song, every announcement, every station identification, written down with the time beside it. Sixty-two lines on a good afternoon. Ramona said the log was the most boring job in the building and also the one they could not run without, and I decided she was saying that to make me feel better.

On a Thursday in March the power flickered. The board went dark for maybe four seconds and came back up, and the automatic system that was supposed to remember what had been playing did not remember anything at all.

Ramona said a word I will not write down.

"We are off the log," she said. "We have no idea what we have played since two o'clock. If we repeat a sponsor spot we owe them money and if we skip one we owe them worse."

I held up my clipboard.

She looked at it the way you look at a door you did not know was in the wall.

We rebuilt the whole afternoon from my handwriting. Two twelve, sponsor spot, hardware store. Two nineteen, song. Two twenty-four, weather. It took eleven minutes and we did not miss a single one.

Afterward Ramona did not say thank you exactly. What she said was, "Sit here," and she moved over, and she showed me what the three left-hand faders did.

I want to be honest about something. For three weeks I had thought the log was busywork they gave to a kid so the kid would feel included. I wrote it carefully anyway, because that is how I was raised, not because I believed in it.

I believe in it now.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Marisol at the Radio Station”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what comparing similar themes and patterns of events across cultures asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Marisol at the Radio Station,” then answer: Transfer comparing similar themes and patterns of events across cultures to a different paragraph or perspective in the reading. What had to change in your approach?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a transfer response and a precise explanation of the adjustment; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If comparing similar themes and patterns of events across cultures is not yet secure, return to “Marisol at the Radio Station” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply comparing similar themes and patterns of events across cultures to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Marisol at the Radio Station.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
